clinicalPearls: Causes paroxysms of sharp, shooting pain in the lateral neck, over the thyrohyoid membrane, radiating to the angle of the jaw, ear, and supraclavicular region
Attacks are triggered by swallowing, phonation, coughing, yawning, or turning the head
A tender trigger point is often found over the thyrohyoid membrane where the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve pierces it
It may follow upper respiratory infection, neck surgery (including thyroid surgery and endarterectomy), or trauma
Diagnostic and therapeutic superior laryngeal nerve block at the trigger point relieving the pain strongly supports the diagnosis
First-line medical therapy uses anticonvulsants such as carbamazepine; repeated nerve blocks or nerve sectioning help refractory cases
The distribution and swallow-triggered pattern distinguish it from glossopharyngeal neuralgia and carotidynia
reference.pathophysiology: Superior laryngeal neuralgia is a paroxysmal neuralgia of the superior laryngeal nerve, usually its internal branch, which supplies sensation to the supraglottic larynx and pierces the thyrohyoid membrane. Irritation, entrapment, or injury of the nerve, sometimes after infection, surgery, or trauma to the neck, is thought to generate ectopic afferent discharges triggered by laryngeal movement during swallowing and phonation. The resulting lancinating pain is referred throughout the sensory field of the nerve, and a focal trigger point overlying its entry through the thyrohyoid membrane is characteristic.
additionalInvestigations: Palpation for a trigger point over the thyrohyoid membrane reproducing the pain
Diagnostic superior laryngeal nerve block with local anaesthetic
Flexible laryngoscopy to exclude a mucosal or supraglottic lesion
Ultrasound of the neck and thyroid to exclude local pathology
MRI or CT of the neck if a structural or neoplastic cause is suspected
Review of any prior neck or thyroid surgery
redFlags: A neck or laryngeal mass suggesting malignancy
Constant rather than paroxysmal pain with systemic features
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and frequently responds to anticonvulsant medication or superior laryngeal nerve blocks, with many cases settling over time; refractory pain can be controlled by repeated blocks or nerve sectioning.
pitfalls: Confusing it with glossopharyngeal neuralgia given overlapping triggers
Overlooking laryngeal or thyroid malignancy as a cause of lateral neck pain
Failing to seek and test the thyrohyoid trigger point
Attributing the referred otalgia to primary ear disease
references: Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery
Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology, Head and Neck Surgery
management: Start an anticonvulsant such as carbamazepine as first-line medical therapy
Perform a superior laryngeal nerve block with local anaesthetic at the trigger point, which is both diagnostic and therapeutic
Offer repeated nerve blocks for pain that recurs after an initial response
Consider nerve sectioning or ablation of the superior laryngeal nerve for refractory pain
Exclude a mucosal or supraglottic lesion with flexible laryngoscopy and treat any identified precipitant such as prior neck surgery or infection
Refer to combined ENT, neurology and pain services for resistant cases
